quote: Female kangaroos, called does, and their relatives give birth to tiny, underdeveloped young, called joeys, that are then carried in a special pouch ... The red kangaroo is the fastest jumper in mammal land, bouncing up to almost 35 miles (56 kilometers) per hour.
unsupported: "born the size of a grape", "crawl into their mother's pouch", "up to 40 mph" (the source gives almost 35 mph)
correctedFact: Red kangaroos are the fastest jumpers among mammals, bouncing along at almost 35 miles per hour. Larger kangaroos can cover more than 23 feet in a single hop at top speed, and they actually burn less energy the faster they hop, at least up to their cruising speed.
extraPoints: Joeys are born tiny and finish developing in the pouch
note: Source says tiny, underdeveloped young carried in the pouch, but gives no grape comparison and no crawl. Corrected fact keeps the speed point, which matches the title.

pageTitle: Octopuses keep surprising us - here are eight examples how
quote: Octopuses have blue blood, three hearts and a doughnut-shaped brain. ... The copper-based protein is more efficient at transporting oxygen molecules in cold and low-oxygen conditions, so is ideal for life in the ocean. ... An octopus's three hearts have slightly different roles. One heart circulates blood around the body, while the other two pump it past the gills, to pick up oxygen.
unsupported: "When they swim," (the source ties the heart roles to no activity); "in deep ocean environments" (the source says cold, low-oxygen ocean conditions)
correctedFact: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood. One heart pumps blood around the body, while the other two push it past the gills to pick up oxygen. The blood is blue because its oxygen carrier, hemocyanin, uses copper instead of iron, which works better in cold, low-oxygen water.
note: The "when they swim" framing is misleading: the heart roles apply all the time.

quote: Kangaroo rats are so well adapted to arid environments that they rarely, if ever, drink water. ... The metabolism of nutrients from these seeds produces small amounts of water. That, plus whatever water is in the seeds themselves, is enough to sustain the kangaroo rat.
note: NPS hedges with "rarely, if ever" drink; the card's "can survive without ever drinking" fits that. Page also places kangaroo rats in North America (Canada, western US, Mexico).

quote: two American-born cats showing the same mutation appeared in Minnesota in 1975 ... the skin of a Sphynx is delicate and not suited to rough play ... Contrary to popular belief, the breed is not always totally hairless and skin textures/degrees of hairlessness can vary. Some short hair is usually present on the nose, ears and tail.
unsupported: "just as sensitive as ours" (source says delicate); "unique 'mustache' whiskers that contribute to their charming personality"; "naturally hairless" is overstated (source says not always totally hairless)
correctedFact: Sphynx cats owe their famous bare look to a natural genetic mutation, but most are not completely hairless: a little short hair usually remains on the nose, ears and tail. Their nearly bare skin feels like warm suede and is delicate, so they suit gentle handling better than rough play.
note: Affectionate personality is supported ("Active, affectionate"). Title "Feline Mustache" rests on the unsupported whisker claim and would need a new title.

pageTitle: Gulf of California 2015, Leg 3 – Biodiversity and Biooptics – Log 6
quote: Bioluminescent dinoflagellates, ostracods, and other planktonic organisms glow after being disturbed by turbulence from the boat. ... The bioluminescent zooplankton in the water light up when they come in contact with the dolphins, and illuminate a perfect outline of dolphin snouts, fins, bodies, and tails. As the dolphins swim along, the bioluminescent lights stream behind them like shooting stars
unsupported: "mainly single-celled" (the source lists dinoflagellates alongside ostracods and other plankton); "blue-green" (the source says blue)
correctedFact: Dolphins do not glow, but they can look like they do. Bioluminescent plankton, including dinoflagellates, flash blue when the water around them is disturbed. Researchers at sea have watched dolphins swim through them at night, lit up in a perfect outline of snouts, fins, bodies and tails, trailing light behind them.
note: Expedition log by a researcher in Steve Haddock's bioluminescence lab at MBARI.

unsupported: All of it: tail movements as a tamarin communication channel, "complex messages", and the comparison to human social networks
note: Searched tamarin tail signaling. The only lead was Moynihan (1970), Smithsonian Contributions to Zoology 28, which has a tail-pattern section among many visual displays, but the Smithsonian repository PDF returned 403 and no other source was found.

pageTitle: Fun Facts About Terrific Sea Turtles
quote: Scientists believe that nesting female turtles return to the same beach on which they were born. Often sea turtles must travel long distances from their feeding grounds to their nesting beaches. Just how sea turtles find their nesting beaches is unknown.
unsupported: "thousands of miles" (the source says long distances)
correctedFact: Scientists believe female sea turtles return to the same beach where they were born to lay their eggs. Getting there often means a long journey from their feeding grounds to the nesting beach, and exactly how they find their way back is still a mystery.
note: NOAA frames natal homing as what scientists believe, not as proven.

pageTitle: What does the new trade ban mean for pangolin conservation?
quote: It is estimated that since 2000, more than 1 million pangolins have been traded illegally at the international level, which would make them the most trafficked wild mammal in the world. Since 2014, all eight pangolin species are classified as threatened with extinction on The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species ... from early January 2017 all pangolins will be listed in Appendix I and international trade in wild-caught pangolins for commercial purposes will be subject to an international trade ban.
unsupported: "taken for their scales and meat" (not on this page)
correctedFact: Pangolins are thought to be the most trafficked wild mammals on Earth, with more than a million traded illegally across borders since 2000. All eight species are threatened with extinction, and since early 2017 every one of them has been under an international ban on commercial trade.
note: The ban covers international commercial trade in wild-caught pangolins.

quote: Their camouflage abilities are due to special color-changing organs in their skin called chromatophores. Chromatophores act as pixels across the cuttlefish's body, changing their size to alter the pattern and color on the animal's skin. ... the skin-morphing papillae in cuttlefish that allow the animal to change the 3D texture of its skin.
unsupported: "in the blink of an eye"; texture change is credited to chromatophores on the card, but the source credits papillae; "mesmerizing underwater performers"
correctedFact: Cuttlefish are masters of camouflage. Pigment organs in their skin called chromatophores act like pixels, changing size to shift the color and pattern of the skin, while small skin bumps called papillae change its 3D texture, letting them match a sandy bottom or a shell-strewn seafloor.
note: Page is from Roger Hanlon's lab institution, which first described the papillae.

publisher: Hawaii DLNR Division of Forestry and Wildlife
quote: ʻĀ (red-footed booby) capture prey by plunge-diving generally from four to eight meters (13 – 26 feet) over the water. In Hawaiʻi, diet is mainly comprised of flyingfish and squid, but also includes mackerel scads, saury, and anchovies.
unsupported: "up to 30 feet" (source: generally 13 to 26 feet); "see clearly underwater thanks to their unique eye structure"
correctedFact: Red-footed boobies hunt by plunge-diving into the ocean, usually from about 13 to 26 feet above the water. In Hawaii they feed mainly on flying fish and squid, and they often forage farther from land than their booby relatives, sometimes in hunting parties with other seabird species.
note: Title "Invisible Wings" does not match the content.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: Box turtles generally live for 25-35 years but have been known to survive to over 100 years old! ... In the northern regions where it gets too cold, they find a comfortable place where they can be somewhat insulated, called a hibernaculum, and will become lethargic, entering a hibernation-like state known as brumation. This begins in October or November and ends in April
unsupported: "one of the longest-living pets out there"; "survive for months without food" (the page describes months of brumation but says nothing about food)
correctedFact: Box turtles usually live 25 to 35 years, but some have survived past 100. In colder regions they spend the winter in an insulated shelter called a hibernaculum, sinking into a sluggish, hibernation-like state called brumation that lasts from October or November until April.
note: Card implies 100+ is normal; the source says 25 to 35 years is typical.

quote: When threatened, the hedgehog raises its quills upright in a crisscross pattern, making its body pointy and sharp. It uses its belly muscles, back muscles, and extra skin to tuck in its head, legs, and tail to curl into a complete ball, protecting its soft belly. ... Hedgehogs can travel up to 2 miles (3 kilometers) a day and move at a speed of up to 6.5 feet (2 meters) per second.
unsupported: "up to 6 miles per hour" (6.5 feet per second is about 4.4 mph); "curl up into little balls for cuddles when they're feeling safe" (the source says they curl up when threatened)
correctedFact: Hedgehogs can scurry at up to 6.5 feet per second, about 4.4 miles per hour, and travel up to 2 miles a day. When threatened, a hedgehog raises its quills and uses its belly and back muscles to curl into a tight ball of spikes that predators find hard to open.
note: The curling claim is reversed on the card: balling up is a defense, not a sign of feeling safe. Title "Cuddle Drones" rests on it.

quote: One spiral tooth projects through the upper lip, jutting nine feet out from only one side of the male's head. It is a tooth, not an antler ... Nweeia and his colleagues have mapped a sensory pathway between that spiral tooth and the narwhal brain, along the way showing how the animal may use its tusk to suss out its environment. ... used a Holter monitor to measure differences in the narwhal's heart rate and found significant changes depending on water salinity.
unsupported: "up to 10 feet" (source says nine feet); "helping these mystical creatures navigate the frigid Arctic waters" (source suggests salinity sensing, possibly linked to ice formation, mating or food, not navigation)
correctedFact: A male narwhal's famous tusk is a spiral tooth that juts up to nine feet from one side of its head. Researchers have mapped a sensory pathway from the tusk to the brain, and a narwhal's heart rate changes when water of different saltiness washes over it, marking the tusk as a sensory organ.
note: Harvard School of Dental Medicine research (Nweeia et al., Anatomical Record 2014).

quote: The Laughing Kookaburra is not really laughing when it makes its familiar call. The cackle of the Laughing Kookaburra is actually a territorial call to warn other birds to stay away. ... The loud 'koo-koo-koo-koo-koo-kaa-kaa-kaa' is often sung in a chorus with other individuals.
unsupported: "echoing through the Australian outback at sunrise" (no timing on the page, and the species lives in eastern Australia rather than the outback)
correctedFact: The laughing kookaburra is not really laughing. Its loud 'koo-koo-koo-koo-koo-kaa-kaa-kaa' cackle, often sung in a chorus with other kookaburras, is a territorial call that warns other birds to stay away. The bird is found across eastern Australia, where its chuckling voice is a common and familiar sound.
note: Title "Rollercoaster Tails" does not match the content.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: The electric organs create strong and weak electric charges, which are utilized for defense, hunting, communication and navigation. ... They are capable of generating up to 800 volts of electricity!
unsupported: "up to 600 volts" (source says up to 800 volts); "enough to stun a horse"
correctedFact: Electric eels can generate up to 800 volts of electricity. Three electric organs make up about 80 percent of the fish's body, and they produce both strong and weak charges, which the eel uses for hunting, defense, communication and navigation in the murky rivers of South America.
note: No horse or 600-volt figure on the page.

pageTitle: Evidence for van der Waals adhesion in gecko setae
quote: The mechanism of dry adhesion in the millions of setae on the toes of geckos has been the focus of scientific study for over a century. We provide the first direct experimental evidence for dry adhesion of gecko setae by van der Waals forces ... geckos use millions of tiny foot-hairs to adhere to even molecularly smooth surfaces.
unsupported: "even run on ceilings" (the paper quotes Aristotle on running down trees head first, not ceilings)
correctedFact: Geckos stick to surfaces with millions of tiny hairs, called setae, on their toes. A 2002 study gave the first direct experimental evidence that this grip comes from van der Waals forces, the weak attraction between molecules, rather than from water, letting geckos cling even to molecularly smooth surfaces.
note: Autumn et al., PNAS 2002.

publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
quote: Cheetahs do not roar, but they make sounds including purrs, barks, growls, hisses and chirps that are unlike those of any other cat. ... Purring: Similar to a house cat's purring. A close-range vocalization that may suggest contentment. It can be heard between mother and cubs. It is unusual in that it may go on for minutes and is produced continuously both while the cat inhales and exhales.
unsupported: "Unlike other big cats" and "the only large felines that never truly roar" (the source says cheetahs do not roar, not that they are the only ones)
correctedFact: Cheetahs cannot roar, but they can purr. Their purr is a lot like a house cat's: a close-range sound that may signal contentment and is often heard between mothers and cubs. Unusually, it can go on for minutes, produced continuously as the cat breathes in and out.
note: The source says cheetahs do not roar but makes no comparison with other large cats.

pageTitle: Mutualism: Eight examples of species that work together to get ahead
quote: Clownfish, also known as anemonefish, are immune to anemone stings, though scientists aren't exactly sure how. ... This means clownfish can safely nestle into the anemone's tentacles to hide from predators. In return, clownfish help the anemone in multiple ways. They keep the anemones free of parasites and provide them with nutrients through their faeces
note: Title "Shrimp Anemone Alliance" mentions shrimp, but the card is about clownfish.

pageTitle: Truncated jarid2 and kdm6b transcripts are associated with temperature-induced sex reversal during development in a dragon lizard
quote: It has a ZZ/ZW system of chromosomal sex determination, but this system is subject to sex reversal of the ZZ genotype to a female phenotype by high temperatures (above 32°C), both in the laboratory and in the wild. Sex-reversed ZZf females are viable and fertile.
unsupported: "It's nature's smart way to balance populations in hot climates!" (not in the source)
correctedFact: Bearded dragons have their sex set by chromosomes, but heat can override it. When eggs incubate above 32°C (about 90°F), embryos with male chromosomes can develop as females instead, in the lab and in the wild, and these sex-reversed females are viable and fertile.
note: First page tried was Holleley et al., Nature 2015 (abstract lacks the 32°C figure); this open-access paper states the full claim.

pageTitle: Sensorimotor synchronization to rhythm in an experienced sea lion rivals that of humans
quote: The only non-human data showing consistent and lagless beat matching to novel stimuli, including music, come from Ronan, a trained sea lion ... Here, we report Ronan's contemporary ability to synchronize head movements with novel metronomic sounds presented at novel tempos. ... This sea lion's sensorimotor synchronization was precise, consistent, and indistinguishable from or superior to that of typical adults.
note: Paper says the only non-human data, which supports "first". The card uses a spaced hyphen as a dash ("consistency - even"), which breaks the site's no-dash rule.

quote: While humans can look to the side just by shifting our eyes, an owl must turn its entire head to look left or right. Each enormous eyeball is locked in one position by bony plates called the sclerotic ring. ... An owl can turn its head 270 degrees in both directions
unsupported: "don't have round eyeballs like us - they have fixed eye tubes" (the source calls them eyeballs locked by the sclerotic ring and does not mention tube shape)
correctedFact: Owls cannot move their eyes: each enormous eyeball is locked in place by bony plates called the sclerotic ring. To look around, an owl turns its whole head instead, as far as 270 degrees in either direction, helped by 14 neck bones, double the number humans have.
note: Card uses spaced hyphens as dashes ("like us - they"), which breaks the site's no-dash rule.

publisher: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (2013)
pageTitle: Shifting mirrors: adaptive changes in retinal reflections to winter darkness in Arctic reindeer
quote: Here, we show that they may have a unique mechanism to cope with winter darkness by changing the wavelength reflection from their tapetum lucidum (TL). In summer, it is golden with most light reflected back directly through the retina, whereas in winter it is deep blue with less light reflected out of the eye. ... Increased sensitivity occurs at the cost of reduced acuity, but may be an important adaptation in reindeer to detect moving predators in the dark Arctic winter.
unsupported: "the only mammals known" (the paper says "may have a unique mechanism"); "eye color" (it is the reflective tapetum lucidum behind the retina, not the iris); "dim Arctic twilight" (paper says winter darkness)
correctedFact: Arctic reindeer change the color of the reflective layer at the back of their eyes with the seasons. In summer it shines golden, but in the dark Arctic winter it turns deep blue, which scientists think boosts sensitivity to dim light, at the cost of sharpness, to help spot moving predators.
note: Stokkan et al. 2013.

quote: On September 10, 1945, Lloyd Olsen ... chopping the head off a chicken named Mike. ... They explained that Mike's reflexes were controlled by his brain stem, which was located almost entirely in his still-intact neck. Further, a blood clot in Mike's severed jugular kept him from bleeding to death. ... Mike lived another eighteen months, got his picture in Life magazine, and made his erstwhile executioner, and his town, famous.
unsupported: "Miracle" (the page names him Mike); "over 18 months" (page says eighteen months); "a famous traveling sideshow attraction" (page says Life magazine and fame, no sideshow)
correctedFact: In 1945, a Colorado farmer chopped the head off a chicken named Mike, and Mike kept living. Experts found his brain stem sat almost entirely in his intact neck, and a blood clot stopped him bleeding to death. Fed with an eyedropper, he lived another 18 months and appeared in Life magazine.
note: Smithsonian Magazine and Britannica pages on Mike both returned 403 to the fetcher; History Colorado was readable.

pageTitle: Fantastic flyers: 10 animals that fly in surprising ways
quote: Also known as parachute frogs, Wallace's flying frogs, Rhacophorus nigropalmatus, live in the thick rainforests of Malaysia and Indonesia. ... They use their webbed feet to glide between trees or to the ground and can travel up to 15 metres this way. ... They have large toe pads which enable a soft landing and help them stick to tree trunks.
unsupported: "parachutes and rudders", "steer mid-air, control its descent" (no steering on the page); "distant" branches is loose (up to 15 meters)
correctedFact: Wallace's flying frogs live in the rainforests of Malaysia and Indonesia and glide between trees using their webbed feet, traveling up to 15 meters, or about 50 feet. Large toe pads give them a soft landing and help them stick to tree trunks when they arrive.
note: Card uses a spaced hyphen as a dash ("leap - it glides").

pageTitle: Hagfish predatory behaviour and slime defence mechanism
quote: Video footage clearly demonstrated that slime secreted by hagfishes fills the mouth and gill chamber of their predators, acting as a very rapid (<0.4 sec) and effective defence mechanism ... at the moment that a predator grasped the body of a hagfish, jets of slime were discharged locally only by those groups of slime glands in the mouth of the predator
unsupported: "up to a liter"; "in just 0.1 seconds" (paper: under 0.4 seconds); "perfect smoky getaway"
correctedFact: When a predator bites, a hagfish fires jets of slime from the glands nearest the attacker's mouth. Deep-sea video showed the slime filling predators' mouths and gill chambers in under 0.4 seconds, so sharks and other fish let the hagfish go and swam off gagging.
note: Zintzen et al. 2011, baited deep-sea video.
